The Basel Problem

Infinite SeriesLimitsRiemann Hypothesis
Game: Add 1 + 1/4 + 1/9 + 1/16 + … and watch the total settle on one exact number.
How to play: Slide to add more terms. Compare the purple line (squares) with the grey one (no squares), which never stops climbing.

Look for the math

Squaring the denominators turns the divergent harmonic series into one with a limit, and a famous one. This was the Basel problem, open for almost a century until Euler solved it in 1735.

It converges

For k ≥ 2, 1/k² < 1/(k−1) − 1/k, and these differences telescope, so S(n) < 2 − 1/n and the sum has a limit below 2. The test confirmed the bound, that the sum only increases, and that it stays under π²/6, for every n up to 100,000.

It is π²/6

Euler's limit is π²/6 = 1.6449…. The same method gives every even power: ζ(4) = π⁴/90, ζ(6) = π⁶/945, and in general ζ(2k) is a rational multiple of π^(2k) through Bernoulli numbers. The test checked k = 1 to 6 against direct sums. No such formula is known for odd powers like ζ(3).

How fast, and a faster way

The tail after n terms is about 1/n, so n × error tends to 1 (the test saw 0.64, 0.95, 0.995, … along powers of ten). That is slow: ten digits would take ten billion terms. But the tail is much closer to 1/(n + ½), and the test confirmed that S(n) + 1/(n + ½) is within 1/(12n³) of π²/6, a tiny fraction of the error. This is the idea behind Euler–Maclaurin summation, which the zeta pages use to compute ζ at complex numbers.

Towards the zeta function

This is ζ(2) in the Riemann zeta function, the sum of 1/n^s. Power 1 diverges (the harmonic series); power 2 converges to π²/6. The Riemann Hypothesis asks about the same function for complex s.

Add 10 terms, then 100. How many more correct digits did the factor of ten buy? And how many does the corrected line gain?
